transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me?

Hi, yeah, thank you for, um, fitting me in. So, I'm here because... well, it's a bit of a massive mess at work right now. I work in human resources, and we've had this incredibly outdated onboarding process for our new hires for years—just completely inefficient, lots of redundant paperwork, and I've been saying for months that we need to overhaul it. 

So, recently, I just... I saw the exact path forward, you know? The vision was just so clear. I pushed ahead with the entire new onboarding launch myself. And I mean, I went all in. I committed a very significant amount of company money, signed off on contracts, and booked extensive vendor time to get their software integrated with our systems immediately. The thing is, I did all of this before any of the actual executive approvals were in place. We have this whole steering committee for procurement that usually takes weeks of endless back-and-forth, but at the time, bypassing them didn't just feel like a good idea, it felt absolutely bold and, frankly, completely necessary to save the company time and drag them into the modern era. I thought I was just taking decisive charge of the situation. 

But, um... well, leadership didn't see it that way at all. They completely panicked when the vendor invoices started hitting the finance department, and now... well, now I'm on administrative leave. And I just keep getting these messages from my director and HR partners basically asking what on earth I was thinking. Which is... it's just really hard to explain to them, or to anyone, because in the moment, it made perfect, absolute sense to me, but now I'm sitting here, locked out of my work email, realizing my entire career might be in jeopardy over this one initiative, and my spouse told me I needed to come talk to someone about it.
During this period when you were pushing forward with the project, did you notice you needed much less sleep than usual but still felt energetic?

Sleep? Um, I'm not really sure I noticed anything specific about my sleep, to be honest. I mean, I wasn't really paying attention to the clock because, well, when you're dealing with a massive system overhaul like this, especially trying to integrate a modern third-party vendor's API with our legacy HRIS software—which, by the way, our IT department hasn't properly updated since maybe 2015—you're naturally going to be putting in some long hours. 

So, sure, I was up late reviewing the service level agreements and drafting the internal communication plans for the rollout, but I wouldn't say I felt like I needed *less* sleep, per se. I didn't feel like I was running on empty but somehow full of energy, if that's what you mean. I was just... working. I was drinking my usual amount of coffee, maybe a little more just to push through the vendor contracts, but it wasn't like I was just wide awake staring at the ceiling for no reason. 

My wife did mention I was spending a lot of time in the home office in the evenings, but I just kept trying to explain to her that this was a critical window. The vendor had a very specific implementation timeline, and if we missed our slot, we would have been bumped all the way to Q3, which would have completely ruined the summer hiring surge. So I was just doing exactly what had to be done to meet the deadline. But as far as actually needing less sleep... I don't know, I haven't really thought about it like that. I just felt extremely focused on getting the project over the finish line.

Would you say this feeling of having exceptional vision and being bold enough to bypass normal procedures is something new that started a week or two ago, or is it more how you've generally seen yourself and operated throughout your life?

Well, that's... that's an interesting way to phrase it. Um, I mean, I've always been a capable person. You don't get to my level in HR without having some degree of, you know, strategic foresight. I've always been able to look at a department's structure and see where the redundancies are, or look at a benefits package and know exactly where we're losing retention. That's just part of the job. I've been doing this for fifteen years, and I've always prided myself on being someone who can see the big picture when other people are just, you know, bogged down in the day-to-day administrative minutiae. 

But this specific feeling... this absolute, undeniable certainty that I had the one true answer and that everyone else's rules were just... obstacles? That's... I don't know. I mean, usually, I'm the one enforcing the procedures. I sit on the compliance committee, for crying out loud. I'm the guy who tells people, "No, you can't just hire your nephew, there's a process." I'm the one who insists on the three rounds of interviews and the background checks and the procurement approvals. 

So, I guess... I guess if I'm being completely honest, no, this isn't how I usually operate. Usually, I'm very methodical. Very by-the-book. But a couple of weeks ago, it was just like a switch flipped. I was sitting in this endless, mind-numbing meeting about the Q3 budget allocations, listening to the VP of Finance drone on about cost-saving measures, and it just hit me like a lightning bolt. I just saw the whole onboarding process in my head, from the initial offer letter all the way to the 90-day review, and I knew exactly how to fix it. And in that moment, the idea of filling out a procurement request form and waiting three weeks for a committee of people who don't even understand HR software to tell me whether or not I could do my job... it just felt absurd. It felt like a betrayal of the company's potential. 

So I just... I just bypassed it all. I felt so clear-headed, so bold, like you said. But looking back, I mean, I've never done anything like that before. I've never committed funds without a PO number. I've never signed a vendor contract without legal review. It's just... it's not me. Or, at least, it wasn't me until about two weeks ago. And now I'm just trying to figure out how I got from being the compliance guy to the guy on administrative leave.

Have you ever had a previous period—lasting a week or more—where you felt unusually elevated, energetic, or on top of the world like this, or conversely, a stretch of weeks where you felt significantly depressed, low, or lost interest in things?

Um, no. No, I really don't think so. I mean, looking back over my life, especially my adult life and my career, I've always been... well, I've always been the steady one. You know? In my department, they actually joke and call me the 'anchor' because I just don't get swept up in things. Like, when leadership announces some massive new corporate pivot and everyone else is running around like their hair is on fire, I'm the guy who just sits down, opens a spreadsheet, and methodically maps out the headcount impact. I don't get overly excited, and I don't get overly dramatic. So, as far as feeling 'on top of the world' or unusually elevated for weeks at a time... no, never. This recent thing with the onboarding project was completely unprecedented for me. 

And as for feeling significantly depressed or low... I mean, obviously, life has its difficult moments. I'm human. Back in 2020, when the pandemic hit and we had to furlough a third of our staff over Zoom... I mean, that was an absolutely miserable stretch of time. I felt terrible. I remember telling my wife I felt like the Grim Reaper of HR, and it definitely weighed on me for a long time. It was exhausting, just emotionally draining to have those conversations day in and day out. But even then, I didn't lose interest in my life, you know? I didn't stop functioning. I still got up at 6 AM every single day, I still made my coffee, I still mowed the lawn on the weekends, and I still took care of my family. I've never had a period where I just couldn't get out of bed or felt completely empty for weeks on end. 

I've always prided myself on being incredibly reliable. I've been at this company for eight years, and before that, I was at a logistics firm for seven, and I think I've taken maybe... what, six sick days total in all that time? I'm just a very, very consistent person. Which is exactly why sitting here right now, on administrative leave, feels like I'm living someone else's life. It just doesn't make any sense because I don't have a history of these massive highs or terrible lows. I just... I've always just been me.

During the past couple of weeks, have you used any alcohol, recreational drugs, new medications, or supplements—including changes in caffeine or energy drink intake—that might have coincided with this shift in how you were feeling?

I know I mentioned the coffee earlier, but just to be completely clear on that, it really wasn't anything out of the ordinary. I mean, my routine has been exactly the same for years. I have two cups of regular drip coffee in the morning—Folgers, usually, nothing fancy—and then maybe, if we have a late afternoon strategy alignment meeting, I might grab a pod from the Keurig in the breakroom. During this whole vendor integration push, I might have had that third cup a little more often, but energy drinks? No, absolutely not. I've never touched those things. You see these young guys in the IT department walking around with those giant neon cans of Monster or whatever, and I just think about the health implications, you know? It's just sugar and taurine. Not for me. 

As for recreational drugs, I mean, I'm an HR professional. I literally oversee our company's substance abuse policy and the random drug screening protocols for our warehouse staff. I've never touched anything illegal in my life, not even back in college. It just wasn't my scene. I'm way too much of a control freak for that, to be perfectly honest. 

And medications... no. I take a daily multivitamin—the gummy kind, actually, because my wife buys them in those massive bulk two-packs at Costco and they just sit on the kitchen counter—and maybe an ibuprofen if my lower back acts up from sitting at my desk too long, but that is literally it. I haven't started any new prescriptions, no weird herbal supplements, nothing like that. 

And alcohol is the same story. I might have a glass of Cabernet with dinner on a Friday night, or maybe a craft beer if I'm out grilling on the patio on a Sunday, but during this whole project sprint? I didn't even have time to think about pouring a drink. I was way too dialed into the implementation timeline. So, no, there hasn't been any change at all in what I'm consuming. Which is exactly what makes this whole situation so incredibly frustrating for me, because if I could just point to some bad reaction to a new medication, or say, 'Oh, I drank six espressos and lost my mind,' it would at least make logical sense. There would be a clear cause and effect. But there's just... there's absolutely nothing like that to explain any of this.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient exhibits a clearly demarcated period (~2 weeks) of abnormally elevated mood with grandiosity ('exceptional vision,' feeling he alone had the right answer), markedly impaired judgment (bypassing compliance procedures he himself enforces, committing significant unauthorized company funds, signing contracts without legal review), increased goal-directed activity (working late nights on the project), and severe functional impairment (administrative leave, career jeopardized). This represents a distinct change from his usual meticulous, rule-following baseline personality, ruling out this being simply his personality style. No psychotic symptoms (hallucinations/delusions of a bizarre or non-mood-congruent nature) were elicited—his grandiosity, while impairing, remained mood-congruent and did not reach delusional intensity with fixed, bizarre content requiring F30.2. Substance/medication use (caffeine, alcohol, supplements) was thoroughly explored and denied as a contributing factor, ruling out substance-induced states. No prior manic or hypomanic episodes, and no prior major depressive episodes meeting full criteria (the 2020 stress reaction did not involve loss of function, anhedonia, or sustained low mood), so this is a first, single manic episode rather than bipolar disorder (which requires a history of recurrent mood episodes). Diagnosis: Manic episode without psychotic symptoms.
